utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry and Mr. Turone for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Zelko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, Defence counsel for Mr. Zelko Mucic. At the same time, I apologise for my colleague Mr. Tomislav Kuzmanovic who will be joining us in the courtroom after the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Salih Karabdic from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, together with my colleague Mr. Tom Moran from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Nancy Boler. I represent Esad Landzo. I am from Houston, Texas. I'm here today with my colleague from Houston, Mr. David Eisen, while Cynthia McMurrey is still out of town. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EISEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will have the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you're still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. McHenry. MIDHAT CEROVAC

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you stated that there were no independent or private units in Konjic. Is it then your testimony that the HOS units and the Splitska Brigade were always subordinate to the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said applied to the armed structures of the municipality of Konjic. I didn't mention the Split Brigade or the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, were there structures present in Konjic that were not part of the municipality of Konjic; I say, "armed structures"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, temporarily. They came to the Konjic municipality. Actually, it was the Split Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I actually don't need you to explain that. I think we've already heard testimony. I just wanted you to confirm it. I think we will be done more quickly if you can answer a question with a simple "yes" or "no" or "I don't know," and then you do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel need not ask questions she does not need the answers to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you regard that as relevant, but go to the areas which really are something.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was General Daidza in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I don't know who you're referring to when you say "General Daidza." I know no one by that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that with respect to the swearing in of the Gijret unit, it was agreed that Mr. Delalic would speak since he had helped provide uniforms. Was it also agreed during the morning briefing, that Mr. Delalic would wear a military costume and that everyone would act as if Mr. Delalic had command authority?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're asking two questions. First, was it decided that he will wear a uniform; second, that he would have authority. Split up your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was it agreed at the morning briefing that Mr. Delalic would wear a military costume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was it agreed that people would act as if Mr. Delalic had command authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you stated, with respect to Celebici, that the prisoners who were brought to Celebici were people who had participated in operations or military operations or had been carrying arms. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have used a term to describe people who participated in operations. These were people who used firearms against the legal forces of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. For us, they were rebels who had violated the integrity and sovereignty of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe you could listen more carefully to my exact question. My exact question was not who were the persons. My question was how do you know the persons, who were brought to Celebici, had used firearms against the legal forces of the state of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, figuratively, there was a struggle. We could hear the shots and there were casualties on our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree with me that it would be a more accurate statement to say that after the military operations in Bradina and Donje Selo, almost all the men were captured and imprisoned, and the sorting out of who participated in the operations and who did not was to take place later; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with your statement, not all of them. When you say "all of them," you probably want to imply that we carried out ethnic cleansing. No. When you say "everyone," that implies women and children and the elderly. I absolutely do not agree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How about if the statement is modified to say men of military age; would you then agree it's a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were rebels carrying weapons of the Yugoslav People's Army, who had been organised in advance and prepared to carry out such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that almost all the military-aged men from Bradina and Donje Selo were captured and taken to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The witness has already answered this question twice as far as he knows. I see no point in asking the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think so. What counsel is asking is whether all men of military age were so taken to the prison. I think that's quite different from what has been said already. Is it true that all those military-aged men were taken to the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the military conscripts were considered by us, to be only the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who recognised the state at the referendum and who, by decision of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, joined the Territorial Defence. The Serb rebels did not do so, and I cannot consider them military conscripts. They were military conscripts on the side of the Yugoslav People's Army and the SDS. They were rebels against their own land, against their own state, the one they were born in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, what happened in Bradina and Donje Selo to those men of military age which were taken to Celebici prison? How did you get to take such men to Celebici prison? This is what counsel is trying to find out because you would have to make a determination about those who you would take to the Celebici prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't present everywhere, at every trench, at every firing position. Evidently, there was a struggle. The Serb forces were assisted from the air. Our forces were shelled. So all those who put up armed resistance among the rebel forces and who, upon capture, were carrying firearms, it is exclusively those men that were taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Does this help your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that only those people, who were carrying firearms when they were captured, were taken into custody; is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has just answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly answer the question? I think you could. It's a simple, straightforward question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it once again?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that only people who were carrying firearms, when they were captured, were taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who upon capture -- there were several ways of capturing people, if you catch him, capture him on the lines, on the front-line, if he is putting up resistance or if he surrendered in his own home where there were weapons. All the weapons were military weapons. According to the formal law, not a single citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia was not allowed, to have in his possession, military weapons, and they had, exclusively, weapons of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is the answer to my question "yes?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer to your question is "yes," but with this addition, that also in homes, in houses, because they also had weapons in their houses and on them, so with this addition that I have just made.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there women who were arrested and taken to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you stated that the MUP took the decision to set up Celebici as a prison. Were you present when the decision to set up Celebici was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the place where the decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: How is it you know that it was MUP who took the decision to set up Celebici as a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know because I was -- I already said in my statement that it was a technical decision made out of necessity. On the 4th of May already, the MUP building and the building of the TO headquarters was hit by grenades, and the only prison that we had in the 70's and the 80's were two premises in the MUP building. This decision was taken out of necessity, and in this MUP prison, there were also some Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, why don't you please listen to my question. My question was not "Why was the decision taken?" My question was "How do you know that it was the MUP who took the decision?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the MUP can take such a decision as part of its competence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you would agree with me that the MUP had no jurisdiction over the Celebici barracks, which was a military facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did MUP have jurisdiction over the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a period of time, yes, but not throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, would you agree with me that, prior to any prisoners being placed there, Celebici was considered a military facility and, indeed, one that had been captured by you and others, as members of the TO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was considered that this facility of the ex-Yugoslav People's Army had been placed under the control of this state and its bodies, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that prior to prisoners being placed there, the TO had jurisdiction over the Celebici facility, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who had authority over it, before prisoners were placed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my prior statement or, rather, the one I made yesterday, as far as I recall, in the Celebici barracks, after the barracks were taken over with the aim of physical security and accommodation, members of the MUP and units of the HVO police were staying there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, are you saying that the TO turned over its authority to the HVO and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it like that. We didn't think about jurisdiction. Our aim was to gain control over that facility. We were not interested in the least who would provide the security for that facility. There were the legal structures, the MUP and the HVO. Our aim was to gain possession of the material that was essential to us and, of course, to place the whole facility under the control of the new state, the new authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, during its existence from May to November 1992, was Celebici a military prison, a civilian prison, something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is not clear. Could you please be more precise?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During its existence, between May and November 1992, was Celebici a military prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A military prison, yes, because in a military prison, there were members of the Territorial Defence who did not carry out certain duties. Like, for instance, they didn't go to the front-lines. They abandoned positions and so on and so forth. There were also some members, some citizens of Konjic, who had committed certain criminal offences and for whom the MUP was responsible, so they had to detain them there because there were no courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, with respect to the Serb prisons, were they in a military prison or were they in a civilian prison or was it mixed at the time, and people weren't concerned about jurisdiction or labels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know is their status. I don't know exactly where they were accommodated. They had the status of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, who was the commander of the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And is it -- am I correct in saying that you don't know who was the commander for the entire period between May and December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not how you put the question to me. Let me tell you. For instance, in 1993, the commander of the Celebici barracks was Mr. Sijacic, a former officer of the JNA and a member of the 4th core.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Between the period May, 1992, and December, 1992, do you know anyone who was commander during that period of the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who do you know who was commander at some point between May and December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who was throughout that period, towards the end of July, I learned that Mr. Pavo Mucic was the director, not the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And how did you learn that Mr. Mucic was the director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned in the Town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You just heard people talking about it, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question, I didn't hear it quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you saying that you just heard general people talking about Mucic's role as commander and that's how you learned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned it in the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence. Purely en person in a conversation. I didn't come to that conclusion at my insistence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And who was your conversation with? Who told you that was Mr. Mucic was commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't recall exactly. There were many people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who was the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know anyone who worked in Celebici as a guard between May and November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I may know one person, his name was Mrndzic, later on he was a member of the 7th Brigade, which I commanded. So I knew him rather well.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And he's the only person that you know who worked in Celebici, at any time, between May and November, 1992, besides Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that it was the only person whom I knew. I also saw some other guys taken out whom I did not know. Once I went to the TO warehouse to look at some 120 millimetre projection. I wanted to see whether the delivery was made in full. It's a large territory, the Municipality in Konjic, I could not know -- 43,000, I could not know everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any persons besides Mr. Mucic and Mr. Mrndzic, who worked in the Celebici prison between May and December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified that the guards at Celebici were not subordinate to Tactical Group 1 or to the coordinator. Please tell us for the period between May and November, 1992, to whom were the guards subordinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, that at first, members of the ministry of the interior were there, as well as the military police. And later on, there were also members of the TO there. And the members of MUP, as is normal, were subordinate to the chief of police and the HVO members, through the HVO commander and the guards were subordinate to the commander of the municipal staff. So these were three separate chains of command in terms of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When was it that the TO had some role in operating Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believed that this happened later on, maybe in October or November. I cannot recall exactly. In November, I was already involved in the establishment of the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it your -- can you be sure, sir, that the TO was not involved in June, July or August? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you specifically when. I remember during the course of our activities at headquarters, there were certain forces from an unit called the Konjic 1. I know that guys from that unit went to provide security for the barracks. I don't know exactly what period this was, but I know that it was from that formation that people went, that is certain forces went to provide the security.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, in July, when you were functioning as the commander of the TO, were the guards in Celebici subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean when I was in the Glavaticevo sector?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I mean during the period, when you were functioning as commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was discharging my duties of the commander, exclusively in the combat activities. I was never in the office. These were combat operations and that was my sole involvement in it, as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, if Mr. Ramic was out of the country and you were functioning in his role in part, who in the TO -- to whom in the TO were the guards subordinate to, during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are making a statement that I cannot understand at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, am I correct that when Mr. Ramic left, he told you to take over as commander of the TO, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Would you want me to quote you, what Mr. Ramic told me through the communications line?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Take over control and command of the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who was taking over the command and the control of the other duties of the TO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The complete activity of the entire headquarters was in the field and that was during the operation at Borci.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do I understand you, that during the operation in Borci, the entire TO staff was in the field and their only duty was combat, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Out of the -- it was also Mr. Tahirovic and Mr. Kevric who remained in the Town of Konjic from the ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So was it Mr. Tahirovic and Mr. Kevric who were taking over as TO commander with respect to duties other than combat duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had some specific tasks to perform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What were their specific task?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tahirovic was tasked with being constantly present at the communications centre. To review from clients, to coordinate with field commanders. That means the commanders who were in charge of the front lines-- I don't know if you know, but we were, we were engaged in a defence of the town and we held lines from which we did not move. He also was in charge of being in touch with the health centre, regarding the wounded, which would be coming from the field. For instance, so that the searchers would be prepared that blood supplies would be ready because this was a daily need. And to report to us regularly, that is to us in the field, what the situation was on the front lines -- defence lines. And as far as Mr. Sefkija Kevric is concerned, his role was based on the duty that he had, and he was a logistics officer and his activity consisted of -- to look after the resources that we had in our warehouses and depots: dry food, ordinance, equipment. To regularly supply us with this material at Mount Prenj. And in the south eastern area of the municipality in the area of Glavaticevo, together with Mr. Delalic, who was somewhere in the middle of that whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So who had responsibility for the Celebici prison, during this time from the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, at that time, I was -- I did not think about Celebici. Madam, I was in a very difficult surroundings at that time. I had a very responsible role to play. And one wrong assessment, one wrong judgement of me was -- could have cost lives of many young men. And my entire mental activity was focused on that. So, my thoughts were not in Konjic, about Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I understand you correctly, during this Borci operation, Mr. Kevric, who was the military logistics officer remained in Konjic and Mr. Delalic became a logistics officer on the front line, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In the field, but not on the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The front line was not far off, but in military terms, the front line is just a bit different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that Mr. Delalic had been asked to participate in this military operation. Who was it who ask Mr. Delalic to participate in these military operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Esad Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: During the time Mr. Delalic was fulfilling these military, did he still have the position as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you would agree and you may have already stated, that the prisoners in Celebici were prisoners of war protected under the Geneva convention, applicable to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be consistent, I'll object the that. That's a legal conclusion and should be made by the Court and not by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Put some other question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was it the opinion of the Bosnia military that the prisoners in Celebici were prisoners of war protected under the Geneva convention, applicable to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He's entitled to say that. And he's a member of the Bosnia military and can say as a fact whether or not they were so considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How did you take those prisoners, which you put in the prisons there? How did you -- what to you is their status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have already stated that several times. They were prisoners of war. They were rebels against the country -- the state, their own country.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you stated that you and others in Konjic paid heed to respect of human rights and international law. It's true, isn't it, sir, that you issued a written order that any time the Serbs shelled Konjic, you would have a Serb prisoner taken out of the Musala prison and killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, I think the Court might want to read this man his rights under Rule 42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear that question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, it's true, isn't it, that you issued a written order that any time the Serbs shelled Konjic, you would have a Serb prisoner taken out of the Musala prison and killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who issued?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: This witness issued. My question is, did this witness issue a written order to this effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, you first said here and you said specifically, and I quote your words, when -- during the -- every shelling, you said, that I said, that we killed some prisoners. In other words, you have just accused me here. You've charged me and I would like to ask the Court to protect me from these allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that true? It's a simple thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not true, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's absolute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that in June of 1993, you were detained and interviewed by, among other people, Agan Nezir?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, objection to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What are you objecting to a question? If he's not detained, he could say so, and find out whatever answer he gives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is not whether somebody was detained or not, all kinds of things happened during the war. It has to do with how the prosecution is using certain documents that under our law cannot be used in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am prepared to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that in June of '93, you were arrested and you subsequently on June 19th of 1993, gave a written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that segment is correct. I was arrested on 16 June 1993. And I could not really recall when it was that I actually gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that you stated in your statement, "On one occasion, I even issued a written order and sent it to all the units and commands, even the 4th core command, the war presidency and the exchange commission to the effect that" --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To the reading of the statement to him? What is it you're objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My objection is to of using the statement, that according to our law, cannot be used. This was an information interview. This is under seal and it cannot be used against any person who gives them. So, in our law, this cannot be used for -- in a court of law. This is something that is given to the police or the investigating magistrate and this is always sealed and this cannot be used and this is the -- this is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, we've heard your objection. Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Would you like me to start again or just start where I left off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Start again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that in your written statement, you stated: "On one occasion, I even issued a written order and sent it to all the units and commands, even the 4th core command, the war presidency and the exchange commission, to the effect that, for every shell fired from the aggressor's positions, I would take out a Chetnik from the Musala detention centre and kill him, for which I had, in fact, appointed a group. After issuing this order, representatives of the 4th core arrived in Konjic and prevented me from doing this." Is that what you stated, sir, in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never stated anything of that kind in June of 1993. And all information interviews which were conducted on this topic were -- never concerned this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may have the usher's assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is his answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to show him a statement and see if he recognises his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think it makes a difference even if he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I certainly want to have this statement introduced as impeachment, so Your Honours can evaluate his credibility. And I think to do that, I have to at least have him recognise his signature. If Your Honours wish me to seek to have it introduced without having him recognise his signature, I can do that. But I certainly think I am entitled, for purposes of evaluating his credibility, to have this statement introduced, solely for purposes of impeachment, not for any other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Impeachment on what respect?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Impeachment on his ability to tell the truth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Of the structure of the (indiscernible) organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I certainly believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You know what evidence he's been giving.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't see the sense in it. Actually, it depends on someone who gives evidence on opinions or things which are not so recorded -- which are not authenticated in any other way. But when the evidence is given all along, noted and accepted and not even disputed, I don't think you need, but it's your position to pursue whatever method you like, but it doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I will point out there are some things that this witness says that are undisputed, but there are some things he stated that are certainly disputed by us and I am going to seek to introduce this for purposes of evaluating his credibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, have you had a chance to look at that document and can you tell us whether or not that's your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to see the original document. We have just received some copies of it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, at this point, I don't believe the original is necessary. If this witness recognises his signature, it's not necessary that we have an original. And I will just remind Your Honours that throughout this proceeding, persons including large numbers of defence witnesses have authenticated documents by using copies and statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise your signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection the witness has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Witness is here, he can say what he wants to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise the signature only on the back page. And during the investigation against me, I never signed any of the records on multiple pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I tender the document -- I don't know the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked Prosecutor exhibit 240.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I object to admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: -- Notes the objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, how many times, approximately, between May and December, 1992, were you in the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, it was the first time, I can't remember the exact date, with Mr. Kevric, to visit a warehouse and to see whether the material we had received were adequate. I was there during the swearing in ceremony. That's as far as I can recall. I may have been on other occasions too, but I remember this swearing in. And in connection with the TO warehouse, where logistics officers and drivers would go often and also in the month of April, when we took over control of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were in Celebici in the end of May, beginning of June, 1992 when prisoners were being brought into the camp and being beaten, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And were being beaten, first put in they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that you were in Celebici at some time around the end of May or beginning of June, 1992 when prisoners were being brought into the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember being in Celebici on one occasion when prisoners were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw that and I was not in a position to see it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you know, what was done to ensure that the persons who worked in Celebici understood the need to treat prisoners humanely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was it his responsibility to teach them?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't ask him if it was his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Well, ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Even if it wasn't his responsibility, he still might know since he was a member of the joint command and the TO staff. First of all, I would just like to ask if he knows and then I can ask if it was his responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if anything was done to ensure that the persons who worked in Celebici understood the need to treat the prisoners humanely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, that I said, that there was an order by the joint command to members of the military investigations commission having to do with correct treatment in the process of presenting evidence, that no coercion should be used and so on. Such an order was drafted and signed by both of the people in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That order was sent to the coordinator, Mr. Delalic, wasn't it also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that it was sent to members of the military investigations commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Can I just ask that the witness be shown Defence Exhibit 145-A5D-18? Just before the Registrar does, can I see it first to make sure it's the right document? Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, does that refresh your recollection as to whether or not the order that you've just referred to was sent to Mr. Delalic, as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is that his order signed by him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's not signed by him, but he has just testified about it, Your Honour. In fact, he testified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How would he know it was sent to the coordinator? This document is not signed by him. Somebody has sent some document to a coordinator. How can he say it was really sent?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, he can certainly say it was directed to and, in fact, he has just stated that it was directed to the investigation committee. In the same way he can testify that it was sent to the military investigation committee, I assume he can state if --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was this document directed to Mr. Delalic as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With all due respect, Madam, the content of this text does not apply to the detainees in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. When you just were referring to a document that was signed by Mr. Ramic and Mr. Zebic, about how interrogations were conducted. Are you talking about a different document than this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you understood me well, I did not say that the document was written in the joint command as to how they would be conducted. That is what you said. I know that a document was written exclusively to the military investigations commission regarding their interviews and interrogations, that they have to be correct, they should not resort to force and so on, but this document, this document refers to the military operation of Bradina. This was probably obtained through intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, you're indicating that there was a different document, not the one that has just been shown to you dated 15th of June, 1992, that was written and given to the military investigations commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It's your testimony that this document dated 15th of June, 1992 had nothing to do with the prisoners in Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with them, according to the contents, according to the wording. Would you allow me to comment on this text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How do you expect him to give you details of a document --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just ask that. Sir, this document before you, is this a document that you drafted or that you saw in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The document has been shown to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about this document. I see this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct that this document, is a document, that you did not draft and that you never saw in June of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what he says. He said he saw it for the first time now. That's what he said. The second question you're asking is not right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But in a statement I said, that I participated in the drafting of documents on behalf of the joint command linked to security of persons, property and areas inhabited by citizens of Serb ethnicity. One such document, I drew up personally, linked to the protection --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I think you have testified about that document and I believe, in fact, Ms. Residovic even showed it to you. I don't think we need you to repeat that. Sir, other than the document that you've just referred to, that we don't have, that was drafted for the military investigation committee, are you aware of any measures taken to ensure that the guards at Celebici understood the need to treat the prisoners humanely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The question is not clear. Did you draft any document directing the guards how they should treat the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I personally did not. That is not my responsibility. My job description is quite different. I'm not working in the security sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it correct then, sir, that you have no idea whether or not any measures were taken to instruct the guards in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think he has made such a claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said he had nothing to do with the security. He just said that. How does your next question arise?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Because he has testified at great length, in direct, about various things, including who the detainees in Celebici were and how they were treated, and I think I'm allowed to ask him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with how the prisoners were to be treated by the guards, the instructions in regard to that. How are the two related, the question you're asking and what his position was? He says he had nothing to do with the security; therefore, he had nothing to do with the prison. So how would he know what instructions were given to the guards?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that you had nothing to do with the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I have given a very brief description of what it was I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me move on. Do you know anything about who, if anyone, arranged for the visits of the Red Cross to the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: First ask him, does he know about the visit of the Red Cross -- you asked the second question but you omitted the first question. Does he know about the visit of the Red Cross to the camp?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not the Red Cross ever visited the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that an international organisation did go to Celebici. I heard something to that effect. I don't know the name of the organisation and I don't know why they went, really. I just heard that they went to inform themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you were in the TO, did you ever see any orders signed by Mr. Delalic, regarding Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And that would include any orders from Mr. Delalic that -- well, let me just go on. Sir, did you ever see at any time between May and November 1992 any orders or any decisions from the war presidency regarding Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you testified, in direct, about a military investigation committee that had been set up. Were you aware, sir, that Mr. Delalic worked with that committee and gave them various instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just know what I have already told you, who were the members of the commission, where they came from, in general terms, and the joint staff did give its signature and everything else. The link to actual instructions, that is something I hear of for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, as a member of the staff, were you aware that after a short period of time in June, Mr. Pajic and other members decided that they could not continue to work in Celebici and wrote a report about the problems in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I only know that Mr. Pajic was withdrawn, to form the military police because he was a former officer of the JNA and he had certain experience in the field. In the meantime, at that time, I was outside Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, then if you were outside Konjic, I take it you don't know whether or not Mr. Pajic was still a member of the military investigation committee at the time he was taken to form the military police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is that supposed to be a question or a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You make such a long statement that includes three or four --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether or not at the time Mr. Pajic was withdrawn to form the military police, do you know whether or not he was still a member of the military investigation committee?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If he was withdrawn, how could he be a member of that commission then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know when Mr. Pajic stopped being a member of the military investigation committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your direct testimony, when speaking about who had authority to release prisoners in Celebici, you reported that some prisoners were released by the military investigation committee. I ask, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of my first conversations with a member of the military investigation commission was held in the second half of the month of July, 1992, in the area of Glavaticevo. The gentleman I was talking to was Nusret Sacibovic. Mr. Sacibovic was a member of the war presidency. He was a member of the military investigating commission and he was a member of the ministry of the interior. When the war broke out, he was an inspector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is it your testimony that Mr. Sacibovic never mentioned that the committee had to stop its work because of mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. During that conversation, which lasted about ten minutes, he didn't mention that. He just mentioned that there were some minor disagreements. He didn't mention any major problems and he didn't mention that the commission was to stop working or that the commission had actually stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that the military investigation committee released certain prisoners? In particular, do you know whether or not it was because it had been determined that they had not participated in any military activities or possessed firearms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my testimony, I have said that during my military training, I never dealt with military investigating commissions, that I was not familiar with the methods used by such investigating bodies, and that's all that I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Were you involved in approving the release of any other prisoners besides the three you mentioned, the two doctors and Mr. Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When Mr. Tahirovic called you, how did you know that these release forms existed? Had you ever seen them? Let me clarify. At the time that Mr. Tahirovic called you, had you ever seen any release forms for prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I hadn't ever. I didn't say, when talking to Mr. Tahirovic, that I knew of the existence of these forms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did you tell him that he should get the forms and send them by courier to your location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said to Mr. Tahirovic, "If there are any papers, forms or any other documents, send them to me by courier, so that I can sign them." I must point out something that is very important and which was, for me, decisive when taking such a decision. First, the fact that I was told this by Mr. Tahirovic, a member of the staff, a man whom I trust because he was a member of the staff, and he explained to me the specific situation in the town of Konjic with regard to the increase of anti-Serb feeling, when the policemen were killed in the village of Bradina, because I gathered the atmosphere he was living in and I took the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will counsel please go straight to the question because his answer has been stated before during his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, I assume that by telling Mr. Tahirovic about what to do, you recognised the fact that you had authority over Celebici prison such that you could release prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct. Your statement is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, certainly you would agree that you had authority to release prisoners at this time, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, then, sir, why was it that you asked Mr. Tahirovic to send you the forms; so that Mr. Golubovic could be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked for them simply because there should be some kind of a trace because I'm not familiar with the actual procedure. There must be some documents on the basis of which a person is released, so I was thinking along those lines. There must be something, some paper, so send them to me, so let's get it over with, because this was his own personal friend and a man belonging to the same generation. We grew up in the same street, me and Mr. Miro Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But you asked him to send in the forms so that you could release Mr. Golubovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was urgent. The situation was specific. I was in a specific situation. I couldn't waste time. Mr. Tahirovic needed to act preventively, in connection with the anti-Serb forces. That is the point. Five policemen were killed in the village of Bradina under unclarified circumstances. The situation was tense in the town itself. Mr. Tahirovic wanted to prevent people taking justice into their own hands, to prevent chaos. You know what chaos means. That would be counterproductive. It would have a negative affect on our own fighters, so on and so forth, and on the citizens of Konjic itself. I must also -- please don't interrupt me. There were Serbs still living in Konjic. Serbs were living there who had obligatory labour, so it was a multi-ethnic town. With my father in the basement was Mr. Nedzo Lojpur.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me, sir, that you could have just asked Mr. Tahirovic to sign the forms on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, listen, we've been for over 15 minutes arguing on matters which are a rationalisation from conduct of the parties. You don't go about asking questions which will not get you anywhere. You ask did you sign the forms, the particular prisoner was released. You don't have to ask further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, the second time you were involved in releases, you stated that Dr. Ahmo Jusufbegovic contacted you, when you were in the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm hearing the French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You must have pressed the wrong button.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, the second time you were involved in prison releases, you stated that Dr. Ahmo Jusufbegovic contacted you. What did Dr. Jusufbegovic tell you about why the doctors should be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Ahmo Jusufbegovic did not explain to me why the doctors should be released. That was the first time I heard that Mr. Petko Grubac and Mr. -- I think his surname is -- I can't remember it now, maybe I will later. Dr. Ahmo is a man of repute and he told me that he had heard, and this for him was news too, that they had been detained in Celebici and as a man of prestige, he had tried to intervene, to contact certain structures. He went to the HVO, but he was unable to do anything. This was maybe five or six days after the case of Miro Golubovic. I'm not sure. I was in Glavaticevo at the time. He said that Mr. Zejnil Delalic himself was with him and that he too was appealing for a solution, for a compromise, that these people should be released and that they were ready to continue their professional activities, to continue treating patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, sir, are you aware that in the latter part of November, Mr. Delic took over for Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? Which duties? I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She is now speaking of Delic, not Delalic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She is now speaking of Delic, not Delalic. She is asking you; are you aware that Delic took over from Mucic as commander of the camp. This is what she's asking you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what month? In what period?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, sir, at any period, are you aware that Mr. Delic took over Mr. Mucic's functions as camp commander or camp director?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time when you had responsibility for any prison camps in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will break here and assemble at 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly find the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Proceed, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am correct that in November of 1992, you became commander of the brigade called the Suad Alic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that no part of the Suad Alic Brigade, or police units that were part of that brigade, were ever responsible for any prison camp in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not how I put it, the way you stated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, how would you put it, sir, was there a time when some part of the Suad Alic Brigade had some responsibility for the operation of any prison camp in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me make a distinction for you between the responsibility and competence. Musala was in competence of the 4th core, the sector of military security and myself as a commander, only was tasked with providing security. Whereas, as a commander of the 7th Brigade, I never established the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: But am I correct that persons under your command were guards at the camp, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware, aren't you, that in December, and January of 1993, Mr. Delic, Mr. Landzo, Bata Alikadic, Osman Dedic and Sead Surcin were in prison in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, to the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not going to get into why they were in prison or anything about that. It's just a foundation because this witness may have had some involvement with the accused related to that. But I will not discuss at all the merits or why they were in prison and I believe it's already in the record that at some point they were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a single document, as I recall, that was introduced, as I recall, and that was just to show people's names and ranks and titles and things like that. Whatever occurred involving my client or others after the time of this indictment, I believe is irrelevant and I believe it's surely irrelevant as to this man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the purpose of the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my next question was to ask whether or not this witness had any direct role in getting the accused released and that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what fact of importance to this case does that make more or less likely? It's totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I can explain more, I don't want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not necessary because I don't think it's a relevant issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I have a point regarding the transcript. At page 43 of LiveNote, line 17, it says Mr. Delalic, and I understood my learned friend to say Mr. Delic, I believe there's an error there. Could that be confirmed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm sorry, I don't have the LiveNote page, but my last question, certainly had to do with Mr. Delic, not Mr. Delalic. Sir, let me just ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just ask you this correctly. Were you part of an armed group which illegally released Mr. Delic, Mr. Landzo and some others?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, same objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this directly goes to this witness' bias, if, in fact, the information is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: First of all asking if --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had asked that question and that was objected and I was asked to go on to a more specific question, so I will go back, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware that in January of 1993, Mr. Delic, Mr. Landzo, Mr. Ali Catic, Mr. Dedic and another person were imprisoned in Celebici, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You want to show some special relationship between the witness and some of the accused persons, this is what you want?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And this is a foundation question for my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: (Reporter wrote MR. OLUJIC:) I am going to object at this point also, on behalf of Mr. Landzo, just as well as my learned counsel had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the question can be answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never a member of what you described as an armed group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You were a member of a group, sir, that had Mr. Delic and Mr. Landzo and the other people released in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January of 1993, I was commander of a brigade, I was not a member of a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, as a member of the brigade, did you participate in a group that forcibly had Mr. Landzo, Mr. Delic and some other people released from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When you are talking about a group, he was a brigade commander. I don't know what you mean by the group. You say that the brigade commander, ask him as a brigade commander so he can --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, in any function whatsoever, in January 1993, did you play a role of having Mr. Landzo and Mr. Delic released from imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't know if this is the proper time, but I have noticed that also there's an error like Mr. O'Sullivan has pointed out in 46 line 9, when I made an objection on behalf of Mr. Landzo, Mr. Landzo's name was not mentioned and also instead of my name, Nancy Boler, as the person who made the objection, they've written Mr. Olujic's they have written Mr. Olujic's name. That was 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, we can see it. Mr. Olujic was entirely innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, they still have on 47.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, was Mr. Esad Landzo ever part of the Suad Alic Brigade or police units that were part of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Correct the witness' microphone now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's a sector in the brigade, which is called an organisation mobilisation affairs centre and they have lists of men. As the commander of the brigade, I was not in a position to memorise 1400 names that were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do I take it that you have no knowledge about whether or not Mr. Esad Landzo was ever a part of the Suad Alic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only do I do not know whether there was Esad Landzo there, but there may have been a number of persons named Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of more than one person in Konjic being named Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe you misunderstood me when I said, when I said other Esad Landzo's, I meant other names and other people and there are several Landzos. I know exactly where the family came from and I know them. It's a large family, there's quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would the witness say that he can't vouch for whether the accused person or any other persons of that name, only persons for that matter, he's a member of his brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why don't you go on to some other question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, given that he, as I understood, he misspoke in his answer, I think I was allowed to clarify that, but I am certainly going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, since you left Konjic, you have been in contact with Mr. Delalic on different occasions, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the nature of work and the nature of his duties and my needs. And it had to do with the work that I have with Mr. Kevric.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, maybe my question wasn't clear, or let me just -- in case it's not. Sir, after he left Bosnia in the end of 1992, since he's been outside of Bosnia, you have continued to be in contact with Mr. Delalic on different occasions, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To maintain contact, linguistically speaking, means to exchange information and I was in no position to do that. In fact, what I did with the citizen, Zejnil Delalic, and I believe this was maybe '94 or '95, I just sent a few letters by certain persons, different persons who were travelling to Austria and Germany and in terms of exchanging information into letters and telephone conversations that we were not able to have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree with me that in discussing your needs, in your letter, in one of your letters to Mr. Delalic, you suggested that he could provide you with some money, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me correct you again on this point. We did not talk. I may have written something to him and I am not even sure whether any of these letters have reached him because I never had any contact with him. Contact was impossible, technically speaking it was. That is through -- by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember in your letter to Mr. Delalic, did you suggest that he should give you some money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that I may have written the first letter after I was seriously wounded. This was -- I was in a special kind of a mental and physical state at the time. If I were to be shown this letter, I may be able to confirm it for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution document 241.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me just direct your attention to the very end of the letter, the third to last paragraph. Sir, does this letter refresh your recollection as to whether or not you suggested that Mr. Delalic should provide you with some money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me read you exactly what I had written. Here it says, let him send me those pills for headache. In other words, medication. And this is in the next sentence, when I say, and if he were to send some money, I would not be "angry." And it is just a local Bosnian way of putting things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would request that his prior statement, that he gave to the Defence, that was previously marked be admitted for, solely for purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's nothing impeachable here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You want this also? You want this also in the last portion, which you rely upon if that is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for purposes of completeness, we would, although I had not yet done it, we would also ask what this letter be admitted into evidence also. So I would be asking that this letter be admitted and that his prior statement to the Defence, which was previously shown to him, for purposes of impeachment, but had not technically been offered into evidence, I would be seeking to have both of those admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this? What are you impeaching?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to this last letter, since he's admitted exactly what he's said, the prosecution thought you might want it for purposes of completeness, but if you don't feel it's necessary, we won't be pressing the matter. We would, however, be seeking, so if Your Honours don't believe it's helpful to have this letter, we won't be seeking its admission. We would be seeking the admission of his prior statement to the Defence, which we show him in examination. It's marked 239. The previous statement in that, we would be certainly seeking for admission because it did impeach this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We raise an objection and we believe that it is not a basis for impeachment. And as far as the second document, we believe that there's no basis for admission of the second document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Our objection is similar and that this letter -- this statement has not been properly authenticated until we object to its admission on that ground. In addition, the witness has denied making that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it's a fair request, there's nothing to impeach him. It couldn't be admitted for any purpose really.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept your ruling on this letter. We would be seeking, though, separately to have his prior statement, Exhibit 239, which I believe the witness did agree, contradicted his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, any re-examination? The last circled exhibit is not being admitted. There's no basis for it really.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I hope, Your Honour, that the statement has not been admitted either because we objected at the time and there was no contradiction as we saw during the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 241, that is not being admitted, but 239 is. Is there any re-examination? Because counsel has gone through the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, the Prosecutor read to you and showed you a statement, which was used in the course of the criminal proceedings against you. Can you tell the court whether the proceedings have ended and how?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the proceedings have been terminated and I was acquitted of the charges.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cerovac, you have also been asked how you knew that people were carrying arms. Tell me, please, whether you and the staff had seized weapons in the homes of the people captured, military weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In answer to the first part of your question, by nature of my job and my training, I knew all the types of weapons used by the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe you didn't understand my question. I didn't ask you how you knew about the weapons, my question is, were weapons found and surrendered to the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were weapons found and seized and handed over to the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the people captured, yes. It was an enormous quantity of weapons, there were about 700 barrels of automatic and semi-automatic rifles. And there were some 82 millimetre mortars and some communications equipment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also asked in connection with the Split Brigade, so could you please, if you can recall, tell the Court whether you know when that brigade arrived and when it left Konjic? You spoke about its composition during your examination in chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mountain brigade arrived in the second half of April and left in the first half of May to the area of Hercnica (phoen).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, during the cross-examination, with regard to the subordination of parts of the combat units of Konjic to Tactical Group 1, my learned friend used several different English terms, so in order to clarify this, these terms may have different meanings, so my question is, could you tell the Court, when the Gijret unit or another unit was transferred to be subordinated to Tactical Group 1 or 2; for how long was it under the command of the commanders of Tactical Groups 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A unit, which is in principal being subordinated to a Tactical Group, is subordinated for the duration of a certain temporary assignment. When the command of the Tactical Groups finds that that unit is necessary or unnecessary for the continuation of the task, when it is found to be unnecessary, the unit is returned to the municipal staff within the original structure, but the municipal staff never eliminates it from its structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When that unit returns, as, for instance, the Gijret unit from its combat assignment, who is it subordinated to, upon its return to Konjic? Which is its superior command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cerovac, was there ever a unit, a part of a unit or a unit, an individual, a soldier from Konjic who was permanently subordinated to the commander of Tactical Group 1, regardless of whether at the time it was Mr. Polutak or Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that this is all we have for Mr. Cerovac. Thank you very much for your assistance and for your resilience. We are grateful for your assistance to the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much. You are discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I be allowed to say a couple of words and to address you personally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness was hurt by some questions put by Ms. McHenry, but I don't think it's necessary for us to go into that again. He has already reacted to the question, so I would suggest that he would not -- he not address the court. But if you grant him permission, he may say it again. He understood questions to mean that he was being charged by this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
