utterances.text: Could Mr. Zejnil Delalic's coordinator make appointments which otherwise were in confidence of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could he make appointments in some other areas where the war presidency had no authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, he could not make any appointments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could Mr. Delalic make any military appointments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already answered that question. He as civilian had no authority whatsoever to make any appointments, military or civilian or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did by this appointment, Mr. Zejnil Delalic become a member of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By this appointment, Mr. Zejnil Delalic did not become a member of the war presidency because the composition of the war presidency was already known and it could not be changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zejnil Delalic's coordinator attend any meetings, any sessions and, if he did, did he have any authority to joining, taking decisions during these sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic could attend meetings of the war presidency only as an exception. And when he did attend, he only had the right to contribute to the discussion, but not to vote.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, do you know whether Mr. Zejnil Delalic at any time during 1992 was appointed or was on duty of the commander of the territorial staff of the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic was never appointed to the, to commander of the municipal -- of the territorial staff of the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who in May, in early May, 1992, was commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was a period when the commanders changed very frequently, but I believe that in early May, the commander was Mr. Esad Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you were to be shown a videotape where Mr. Zejnil Delalic is being introduced as a commander TO and this is in the middle of May, 1992, would you say that this introduction was true or false?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever were to introduce Mr. Zejnil Delalic during this period as commander of the TO headquarters would be saying -- will be stating a false thing. It simply is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, during 1992, did you know the fact that there was a journalist who introduced Mr. Zejnil Delalic in such a manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of this fact. That is, we -- we were able in Konjic to get TV programs broadcast by Croatian television. And in one of these programs, which was named, "Slikom Na Sliku", that is image on image, Mr. Zejnil Delalic was a guest. I personally watched this broadcast and I believe that it was either the programme director or somebody else in charge of this broadcast, did misrepresent Mr. Delalic's title. It was -- we laughed when we saw this because we knew at that time who the commander was, so this was not true. Because at that time, Mr. Delalic was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, did you know on what business was Mr. Delalic on at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that time because he was there on official duty. He had received authorisation as a civilian to do some logistics work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, until when was Mr. Delalic on this duty of coordinator to which he was appointed to the war presidency on 18 May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic was on duty of coordinator, which is the duty that he was appointed to by the war presidency up until 26 July, 1992, when Mr. Delalic assumed the duty of a logistics officer for the Borci operation. And by leaving to that location, his duty of coordinator did not cease.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There may be an interpretation issue. Page 117 of Live Note, line 9, it's 26 July, 1992, could that be verified to see whether the witness said 26 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, he did say 26 July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: June, June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said 26 July. Well, he can correct himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We got a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on June, not July, it was in June, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You -- I want to bring you back to the point where you left off, that his role of coordinator did not cease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic continued on the same -- with the same tasks which involved logistics, logistical activities within, as part of the Borci operation and he continued with the same activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, let me take you back to some other activities in which Mr. Zejnil Delalic was involved while on duty as coordinator, can you illustrate several things that you remember Mr. Delalic being engaged in around June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can indeed and I'll do it gladly. Mr. Delalic was involved in providing security for the warehouse facilities where different types of equipment were stored. And, in this way, he also put his own house as well as the house of his sister at disposal for these purposes. He also invested part of his own personal means to provide certain equipment. He was also involved in setting up communication systems. And when I say this, I have in mind the opening of the railroad tracks between Pazaric and Jablanica, which all had to do with enabling persons and goods to be transported, which was all in the function of the defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So these were some of the activities. Now, Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, just since you said Mr. Zejnil Delalic could not issue military orders, did you during 1992 perhaps see certain orders which were signed by military commanders and were also a signature of the coordinator that was featured, can you perhaps explain us why that signature would have been placed on documents of this type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this would happen occasionally, that in some documents his signature would also feature. But this signature only meant that he was present there because he was a person who was supposed to transmit certain information to the war presidency from the command post or vice versa. And in no way did that mean that he could take decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turning to the preparation and execution of the defence. What were -- what was the role of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency has the highest body of power was involved in a whole range of activities relating to the Defence. The most important among them were securing the maintenance of the vital functions of this town in order for it to survive, which involved, for instance, supply, keeping the water supply going, keeping the electrical power supplies going, then maintenance of the health services, functioning of the social care, functioning of certain institutions such as the Red Cross and a whole range of other activities, which were vital for the functioning of a municipality in the, in the period of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among responsibilities which you just mentioned, did war presidency also have a role in the command and control of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency had absolutely no authority or powers with respect to the control and command of the military forces because it was a civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, given that you were dealing with a whole range of problems, did you at some point have a session of the assembly at which you addressed these issues and did you reach a decision on those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tend to say that, those days, I was on duty, I was on call for 24-hours a day, so we really worked continuously. I slept in my office. There was a metal cot there and so there were times when I did not see my family for 20 days in a row.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, I am now going to show you some documents, they are -- they relate to our proceedings and let me show -- it's 236, D-14. And I have enough copies for the court, so if he would please distribute them around. The transcript reflects "236." It is 136. Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, is this document signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You recognise your signature on this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the witness recognised the document which he has signed in his own handwriting, I am offering it into evidence as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, it is entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we address some of these conclusions, let me just ask you, Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, did the war presidency have any authority regarding the arrest, detention and custody of any persons who were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer to this question is no and absolutely not. The war presidency had no such authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you know who had the authority to arrest and detain persons in those days in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that. These were the bodies of the ministry of the interior, that is, the police as well as the HVO -- the military police and, later on, the TO military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, can you tell me whether during this period, that is, in 1992, the war presidency had any authority in the establishment of prisons or any authority over the prisons which had already been established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The war presidency had no authority. It never established or did have any authority in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the president of the war presidency, did you know whether there were any prisons in Konjic before the beginning of war and at the very beginning of war, if there was a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konjic is a small town, and before the war, it did not have a prison. Within the police precinct building, I know that there were two rooms in which persons who had been arrested or detained were placed, but only for a short period of time, until they were transferred to the district prison in Mostar where the prison was located. There were also similar prison facilities in Zenica and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Considering the combat activities in wartime, can you tell me, Mr. Hadzihuseinovic, whether in the spring of 1992 it was possible to take persons who had been detained, to transfer them to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was absolutely not possible because, at that time, Mostar and the entire Eastern Herzegovina was occupied by the military forces of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, was there a court in Konjic and was there a public prosecutor's office there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer that question in the affirmative. Before the war, there was a basic court in Konjic as well as the public prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said the case referred to Sarajevo and Mostar. You already have evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I only want to ask the president, as he was the president of the municipal assembly, whether the assembly and the war presidency were authorised, in absence of court, whether they were authorised to establish a court. This is my question to the chief officer of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The chief officer has said that the courts are not even functioning. We already have evidence of that. Don't cover the field which has already been covered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Shall we go on or shall we conclude for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you're tired, we will conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not particularly tired. I could go on for another two minutes for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think there is no point continuing now. We will adjourn now. Tomorrow morning, we will not reassemble before 10.45. The Trial Chamber will reassemble at 10.45. Please read back what you might have done so that you do not keep on repeating the same evidence all over again. It will help you think more clearly. We can now adjourn until 10.45 a.m. tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of May, 1998 at 10.45 a.m.
